title: Name That Test
blurb: Six testing disciplines a model runs through before it ships. Sort each scene into the discipline it's exercising.
source: AIGP BOK III.B · AIGP Study Guide (SG) §Domain III.B (Plan and Perform Training & Testing)
hint: Ask what the scene is checking for, not just what data it uses. Validation here means one thing only: does the model generalize beyond what it trained on. The dataset that supplies a model's final, unbiased error estimate is a different concept entirely, tested head-on in Pipeline Twins.
note: These are development-time and pre-release checks. What happens after a system goes live and stays live is a different board.
traps: Scoring an issue by probability times severity is a risk-management prioritization tool, not a performance test — the planted wrong answer for 'which of these does NOT evaluate performance'.

Minimizing human involvement when testing a model against live personal data is never a best practice — oversight has to stay in the loop even during testing, alongside anonymizing the data and scoping tests to intended uses.

zones.name: Unit
zones.def: Checking one component of the pipeline by itself — a tokenizer, a normalization function, a scoring routine — before it is ever wired into anything else. Catches errors while they are cheapest to fix.

zones.name: Integration
zones.def: Exercising components together end-to-end, watching for failures that only emerge once pieces are combined — mismatches, bottlenecks, or bias that no individual component showed on its own.

zones.name: Validation testing (generalization)
zones.def: Checking whether the trained model generalizes beyond the data it trained on: the gap between training-set behavior and behavior on data it has never seen. A development-time check against overfitting — not the model's last word on performance.

zones.name: Performance
zones.def: Measuring the system against the specific, pre-defined metrics — accuracy, reliability, fairness thresholds — that translate the project's business, ethical and regulatory goals into numbers everyone signed off on.

zones.name: Security
zones.def: Probing whether the model can be attacked: weights stolen, training data reconstructed, outputs manipulated by crafted inputs. Resilience against deliberate or accidental compromise.

zones.name: Bias & interpretability
zones.def: Checking whether outcomes are fair across protected groups, and whether a decision can be explained in terms meaningful to the people who have to rely on it.

items.label: The tokenizer alone is checked for crash-free handling of emoji input.
items.why: Single-component isolation is this discipline's whole job — the tokenizer either handles the input or it doesn't, independent of anything downstream.

items.label: A function that standardizes how different data points are represented is checked entirely on its own, before it's wired into anything downstream.
items.why: Isolating one building block catches errors while they're cheapest to fix, before a subtle flaw scales across millions of records and quietly skews results — the discipline stays here even though the function will later run as part of a larger pipeline.

items.label: A custom scoring routine buried in the pipeline is run against a handful of known inputs and checked line-by-line for the right output, before the rest of the system even exists to call it.
items.why: Checking one routine's output against known-correct values, before the rest of the system exists, is the narrowest and earliest gate — distinct from the next discipline, which only starts once multiple pieces are wired together.

items.label: Retriever, model and UI are exercised together end-to-end; emergent failures appear only at this level.
items.why: Failures that only appear once components run together are this discipline's signature — no single-component check would have caught them.

items.label: An inventory system's pieces pass cleanly on their own, then the whole thing starts over-ordering products tied to certain demographic groups once every component runs together.
items.why: The problem only surfaces once the full system is combined, so the fix has to be applied at the combined level too — a component-by-component review would have missed it entirely.

items.label: A loan-approval model returns different results on different hardware, because of floating-point precision differences that only show up once the full system runs end to end.
items.why: The discrepancy is a byproduct of combining components on real hardware — governance response is to document the variance range and set acceptable decision boundaries, not to chase it out of any one piece in isolation.

items.label: Great accuracy on the data it trained on, poor on records it has never seen.
items.why: This is the generalization check — the gap between training and unseen-data behavior — distinct from the test/holdout set, which stays untouched until tuning is finished and then supplies the model's final, unbiased error estimate.

items.label: A model hits near-perfect accuracy on its training set, then performs inconsistently once new patient groups outside that set are run through it.
items.why: The training-to-unseen-data gap is exactly what this discipline exists to catch; a fairness metric would instead compare error rates across protected groups on the same dataset, which this scenario never does.

items.label: One model's predictions swing wildly depending on which slice of the training data it sees; another barely moves off the average no matter what's fed in.
items.why: Wide swings across training slices versus flat indifference to the data are the two failure signatures this discipline watches for during development, well before anyone talks about a final performance number.

items.label: Response-time disparity is measured across user regions under load.
items.why: Processing-time equity turns a business/fairness requirement into a measurable, pre-defined metric — distinct from a protected-attribute-flip check, which watches output content, not latency.

items.label: Statistical sampling and decision-analysis checks are run against the system's outputs to confirm they meet the accuracy and reliability targets set at the start of the project.
items.why: Statistical sampling and decision analysis are recognized ways to test whether a responsible AI system meets its targets; scoring an issue by probability times severity is a risk-management prioritization tool, not a way of testing the system itself.

items.label: The fairness and reliability numbers a project signed off on months ago get checked against what the system is actually producing today, using the same metrics everyone agreed to.
items.why: Holding results to the metrics agreed on up front, not whichever number happens to look best, is what keeps this discipline honest and prevents teams from quietly swapping in a flattering measure.

items.label: An outsider probes whether a specific patient's record was in the training set.
items.why: An outsider learning whether a specific record was in the training set is a security-testing failure — distinct from the generalization check, which only cares about accuracy on unseen data, not who was in the training set.

items.label: Penetration-style checks look for ways an attacker could steal the model's weights or reconstruct pieces of the training data.
items.why: Targeting weight theft and training-data reconstruction is an attacker's-eye view, distinct from a generalization check, which never considers whether anyone is trying to extract anything from the model.

items.label: Penetration testers find that carefully crafted inputs can flip an already-accurate model's diagnosis in roughly one case out of eight.
items.why: Crafted adversarial inputs causing misclassification is a security-testing finding; governance response is to document it as a known limitation and add input validation and anomaly detection, not to wave it off because clinical accuracy still meets target.

items.label: Protected attribute flipped, everything else held constant, output watched.
items.why: Watching whether flipping a protected attribute alone changes the output is a counterfactual-fairness check — distinct from a membership-inference probe, which asks whether a record was in the training set at all.

items.label: A hospital's compliance file shows fairness checks were run and logged, plus a record that decisions could be explained to reviewers — evidence the organization met its duty of care.
items.why: Logging that fairness and explanation checks actually ran is what turns them into defensible regulatory evidence — distinct from a security audit trail, which documents attack resistance, not fairness or explanation quality.

items.label: A model's decision gets translated into terms a clinician can actually act on, not just a probability score.
items.why: Translating a decision into terms a stakeholder can use, rather than leaving it as a bare probability score, is the half of this zone a black-box model can still fail even after passing every accuracy and fairness number.
